meta.title: The New Market Structure: AI Concentration and the Largest Hedge Fund Degrossing in 10 Years
meta.thread_line: 7 threads · October as a hedge fund degrossing · strikeout-strikeout-home-run market structure · AI financing, credit and rates · Anthropic's S-1 · memory, optical and his positions · Eli Lilly · Bitcoin, quantum and tokenization

snapshot: October's tech sell-off was a **rotation and a record hedge fund degrossing** (Morgan Stanley Prime Brokerage's largest), not a breakdown: S&P -93 bp for the month, 9 of 11 sectors up, share of names above the 50-day average from 20% to 61%.
Visser's frame: market structure has changed for good, so expect "strikeout, strikeout, strikeout, home run"; exiting on bubble fears risks missing the few months that make the whole return.

The hyperscalers moved from debt-free cash machines to heavy borrowers (~$1T of AI debt this year); Goldman sees financing needs peaking in 2027 and the constraint as investor absorption and concentration, not demand.
Oracle's cash-flow-positive plan and Anthropic's S-1 ($130B+ cash) are read as signs external financing needs may be peaking; compute is in contango and GPU rental prices are rising.

He rebuilt his Micron position, added optical names, holds silver and Eli Lilly (which he says will be the S&P's biggest stock before the end of 2030), and advises trimming hyperscalers for agentic compute.
Rates are the pressure point: CCC yields ~16%, mortgage rates up 100 bp since April, and the Nov 4 Treasury refunding is a catalyst he thinks is under-watched.
Bitcoin fell 4% on the week and wasn't hacked in the Binance theft; he is long Bitcoin versus short NDX and puts the odds of a quantum break by Dec 2028 at 15%.

themes.title: October was a hedge fund deleveraging and rotation, not a crash
themes.lead: Morgan Stanley's largest-ever degrossing hit a concentrated AI trade while the broader market quietly rose.
bullets: The S&P fell 60 bp on the week and **93 bp** for the month; 9 of 11 sectors were up and the share of S&P names above their 50-day average went from 20% to 61%.

Morgan Stanley Prime Brokerage reports its largest degrossing; Charlie McElligott's pair-trade monitor shows 124 pair trades unwound, 47 with moves beyond three sigma, in a year of widely high Sharpe winners that were almost all AI.

The 4% S&P drawdown most resembles the GameStop hedge-fund unwind inside a good economy; every other drawdown of 6%+ was 15%+ and tied to recession or tightening. The VIX barely budged (above 20 on Friday, then back) and IG CDX shows no credit panic.

Goldman's AI long-short basket (winners vs losers) gave back the whole year and the SMH fell to its 200-day, held it, and is the pattern of hedge funds getting over their skis; hedge funds are still up for the year in aggregate.

Technicals: head-and-shoulders and island-top shapes explain the bears, but the monthly charts look fine; average 14-day RSI of his 100-name agentic index hit the year's low; the VIX needs ~16 to signal calm. He expects no re-leveraging soon.
Screen idea: he runs weekly technical sheets through an LLM for names in advance or pullback with a rising MACD histogram above an upward-sloping 200-day; only five names fit.

quote.text: Picking the end of a hedge fund deleveraging is not easy.

themes.status: MARCH VIDEO: LEAVING THE QE WORLD
themes.title: Market structure has changed: strikeouts, then a home run, and borrowing hyperscalers
themes.lead: The hyperscalers left the debt-free QE world and now trade like leveraged bets; staying out risks missing the few months that matter.
bullets: Nvidia returned about 30% annualized over roughly 30 months, and a single four-month stretch made the entire move; fewer than 15% of months drove it. The S&P shows the same shape: one run from September produced 150% of the return over 13 months.

In March he argued the market was leaving the SaaS/Google/Amazon/Meta world of no debt and always-beat earnings for one of higher oil, rising rates, credit spreads and volatility, like the emerging markets he lived through.

The four hyperscalers (Amazon, Microsoft, Google, Meta) are flat relative to the S&P since 2020 and flat since October 2025; this week Google fell 12% relative to the S&P, its biggest relative drop back to the financial crisis.

Single-day wipeouts this year: Google ~$500B, Microsoft $357B and Nvidia on DeepSeek $589B (about 20% of the whole Russell 2000). Microsoft is now the best performer because it is the one that hasn't raised capital.
Hyperscalers and the AI semis trade used to be uncorrelated (trade was underpriced); now they are locked together, so doubting hyperscaler capex means doubting memory and semis too.

Advice for his RAAS/FAS followers: trim hyperscaler weights, add agentic compute, keep longevity (Eli Lilly) and energy; rates stay higher and long-term yields probably peaked. Apple holds a ~40 P/E on a quality balance sheet with no spending.

themes.title: AI financing is the binding constraint, and rates decide the pace
themes.lead: Demand is not the issue; absorption, concentration and long-end rates are.
bullets: Goldman (Allison Nathan interview, August): financing needs peak in **2027**; the constraint is investor absorption and concentration. Insurance demand for long-duration debt fell ~50% because of overexposure to 10 or so names; private markets and SPVs, with ~$4.5T of buying power, fill the gap.

About $1 trillion was raised this year across 16 companies (Meta, SpaceX via SPV and others), falling as rates rose; AI capex is 27% then 33% then 35% of the IG market through 2027. Microsoft announced a $25B deal and its CDS stayed calm because it hadn't borrowed.

Oracle had its best CDS week since September 2025 and the biggest tightening on record after pledging no more than $20B of extra financing through 2030, free cash flow positive in H2 2028 and $30B by 2029. Gavin Baker (TBPN): external financing for AI may be approaching a peak. CoreWeave debt also handled news well.

Compute has moved into contango and GPU rental prices are rising; Baker says future capacity is getting more expensive. Visser says capex guidance of $196B vs $185B is irrelevant next to the buildout.

Rates: the 10-year peaked around Oct 7 and broke its 50-day, with 4.50% a possible target if Bessent errs at the refunding; mortgage rates are up 100 bp since April (60 since Jackson Hole); CCC yields are ~16%, wider than 2022, so he expects bankruptcies.

Catalyst: the quarterly refunding on Nov 4. Citi expects Bessent to cut long-bond sales; Visser sees a possible twist or yield-curve-control-like shift if 20- and 30-year auctions shrink. Fed hike odds stayed near 75% for December, which he thinks isn't a given.
Goldman also shows energy, tariff and software inflation effects rolling off, and year-over-year DRAM prices collapsing; Intel was hit by memory costs.
themes.watch: Visser deliberately held the August Goldman interview until Oracle's news; Musk's "guppy level death" warning for neoclouds comes as he raises $40B (Visser's reading is that he wants to crowd out rivals).

themes.title: Anthropic's S-1 removes most of the IPO risk
themes.lead: A $130B cash balance and fast growth mean Anthropic needs less financing than the bears assumed.
bullets: The S-1 shows **$132B** of cash, a surprise given the trillion-plus raised for AI this year not from free cash flow; revenue grows much faster than expenses and enterprise adoption is early, with half the Fortune 500 already customers.

Chamath said the IPO should be at a trillion dollars because of capital needs, then revised it: the company needs far less financing, so 1.3-1.7T. Hyperliquid's pre-IPO market traded around 1.7T Saturday. David Sacks, not an Anthropic fan, argued the capital backs its capex commitments to 2030.

Visser's own ChatGPT run on the S-1 gave a base case of ~$100B (95-110). Versus Google's S-1, Anthropic's prior full-year revenue was 1.4 vs 4.5 and its growth is far steeper; the October number was left blank, which Gavin Baker reads as likely strong.

He still doesn't want to own it: a hard business with commoditization, and he now uses ChatGPT, Grokbot and Muse more than Claude; Gemini impressed him this week. Opus 5.5 is a step up, and withheld better models limit distillation.
On Sam Altman's Cheeky Pint comments about building data centers and open source: not simple with memory shortages.

quote.text: it is a very hard business to be fighting up in commoditization.

themes.status: MICRON BACK UP · OPTICAL · ELI LILLY
themes.title: Memory, optical, robots and Eli Lilly: where Visser is positioned
themes.lead: He sold Micron in March or April, rotated to silver and crypto, and bought AI and optical names back this week.
bullets: Micron: first sales since March or April, most proceeds went to silver and crypto, but his position is back to a decent size after SK Hynix's numbers and Astra bringing humanoids closer. Memory contracts now run to 2030 with no slowdown; Micron fell 40%.

Elon Musk: robots will need huge onboard RAM for vision and planning, so robots could become the largest RAM consumers; Visser's sequence is coding agents this year, consumer agents from September, embodied agents next year, citing a report that GPT6 may bring robotics a "ChatGPT moment".

Corning's earnings: optical connectivity could expand 10x per GPU, accelerating in 2028, with supply constrained (a Vera Rubin story). He has been buying optical on the bounce; one large optical holding (name garbled) he won't sell unless a rumored merger with another company happens.
Silver: not the best rotation, down big, but he still likes it for the embodied phase, central bank and tech buying, with CTAs heavily short. EWZ had a historic fall.

Eli Lilly: Q3 revenue +39% to **$24.4B**; US GLP-1 penetration ~10% of 110M obese or overweight, international ~2%; prices falling and volume rising (Jevons). CEO Dave Ricks took Musk's side on a VC's longevity bet. Visser: "I think this will be the biggest stock" in the S&P by end of 2030; it is number nine now.
themes.watch: These are Visser's own holdings and trades; he discloses the Micron, silver, EWZ, Lilly and optical positions and that the memory trade has lost money recently.

themes.title: Bitcoin shrugs off the Binance hack; quantum risk and tokenization
themes.lead: Bitcoin barely moved on the largest crypto heist, and Visser stays long it against the Nasdaq.
bullets: The Binance theft, the largest ever, was not a hack of Bitcoin; Bitcoin fell **4%** on the week and the day showed no trace. October: Nasdaq 100 down 16.5% vs Bitcoin down 7; it is still up 25%.

Trade: Elliott-wave count shows a classic five-wave move and a 38% retracement of wave four; he favors long Bitcoin, short NDX. It has traded correlated to the SMH since the fifth-wave top, with oil and 10-year yields as the other drivers.

Quantum: a quantum company (name garbled) claims it will break the cryptography by 2028; Visser fed the claims plus Google, IBM and others into ChatGPT, which gave about a 15% chance of getting there by December 2028.

AI hacking is global, including Forex brokers in Japan. Tokenization: his prompt covered Ondo, Centrifuge, Figure and others; Google is building a Bitcoin and crypto custody service for institutions, Solana RWA hit a record and the DTCC tokenization service is live.

takeaways.title: Read October as a rotation and degrossing; check breadth (names above the 50-day) before calling a top.
Stay invested through bubble fears; the few best months carry most of the return.
Watch the Nov 4 Treasury refunding, the 10-year near 4.50 and CCC spreads as the real stress points.
Track hyperscaler CDS and Oracle/Anthropic cash flow for signs financing needs have peaked.
Look at memory and optical (Micron, SK Hynix, Corning) as the embodied-agent trade, but size for the 40% drawdowns.

claims.claim: Eli Lilly becomes the biggest stock in the S&P 500.
The Anthropic IPO happens in about two weeks.
The Anthropic IPO prices in the $1.3-1.7T range.
There is a 15% chance quantum computing breaks Bitcoin-class cryptography by December 2028.
AI financing needs peak next year.
Oracle turns free cash flow positive in H2 2028 and reaches $30B in 2029, raising no more than $20B more through 2030.
Optical connectivity per GPU expands up to 10x, accelerating in 2028.
Bessent cuts US long-bond sales at the quarterly refunding.
The 10-year Treasury yield can fall toward 4.50%.
About $90 trillion of AI-related spending will happen.

other_news.title: Microsoft offered to buy out 60,000 workers (27% of staff); revenue per employee is soaring and headcount would fall to 2020 levels, which Visser calls stage one of AI's labor-versus-capital issue.

S&P earnings growth ~30% vs ~25% expected, with guidance stronger than last quarter; Europe's earnings growth rivals the US for the first time in years. Jensen Huang's "$90 trillion, not 10 guys" capex broadening is a source of debt demand.

Sources referenced: Morgan Stanley Prime Brokerage, Charlie McElligott, Goldman Sachs (Allison Nathan), Gavin Baker on TBPN, Chamath, David Sacks, Citi, TrendForce, Mike Wilson, Mark Whailing, All-In on the S-1.
TLT is flat since the hawkish speech by Kevin Warsh; inflation expectations on swaps haven't moved in a year, and DRAM prices are collapsing year over year.
